How Michigan property tax is calculated

Michigan assesses property at 50 percent of its true cash value, and that half-value figure is the state equalized value (SEV). Tax is not charged on SEV directly. It is charged on taxable value, which for each parcel is the lesser of two numbers: last year's taxable value (less losses) multiplied by 1.05 or the inflation rate, whichever is smaller, plus additions, or the current SEV (MCL 211.27a).

This is the Proposal A cap. It is why two neighboring houses of equal market value can carry very different bills. A long-time owner usually pays on a taxable value well below SEV, and that cushion goes with the owner, not the parcel. Most sale-day tax surprises in Michigan trace back to this one rule.

  • SEV is half of the assessor's estimate of true cash value.
  • Taxable value grows slowly while the same owner holds the parcel.
  • Each local taxing unit sets a millage rate, and that rate is applied to taxable value to produce the bill.

What happens to taxable value when the house sells

A transfer of ownership resets taxable value. For the calendar year after the transfer, taxable value becomes the SEV, and the 5-percent-or-inflation cap then applies again from that new base (MCL 211.27a(3) and (4)). Transfer is defined broadly. A deed, a land contract, certain trust changes, and a distribution under a will or by intestacy all count.

An heir who is the decedent's spouse, parent, child, sibling or grandchild can take a home without the reset, as long as it stays residential (MCL 211.27a(6)(f)). A land contract counts as a transfer on the day it is signed, so the deed that follows does not trigger a second reset.

The new owner files a State Tax Commission form with the local assessing office. It lists the parties, the date, the real price paid and the parcel number or legal description, and it is due 45 days after the transfer (MCL 211.27a(10)). The register of deeds also passes recorded deeds to the assessor at least monthly, so the reset does not wait on that paperwork.

Board of review and Tax Tribunal appeals

The first stop is the local board of review. It meets the second Monday in March, and a city or township may choose the Tuesday or Wednesday after that as the starting date. The opening session begins no earlier than 9 a.m. and no later than 3 p.m. and runs six hours or more. Across that week the board sits 12 hours, three of them in the evening (MCL 211.30).

An owner or an agent can ask for a corrected assessed or taxable value, and the board must correct it if sufficient cause is shown. A nonresident can protest by letter, and a township or city may allow resident protests by letter too. The board mails its written decision, with a notice about the tribunal, no later than the first Monday of June.

The Michigan Tax Tribunal hears the next level. For a house, the petition goes in by July 31 of the tax year, and the same date covers agricultural and timber-cutover land. Commercial, industrial and developmental real property, plus related personal property, has an earlier May 31 date. Other matters get 35 days from the final decision. A residential valuation case generally starts with a board of review protest. Disputes limited to arithmetic mistakes on a bill get 60 days from the treasurer's mailing (MCL 205.735a).

Principal residence exemption when you sell

The principal residence exemption (PRE) removes the local school operating tax from an owner's home. An owner claims it by filing a Principal Residence Exemption Affidavit, Form 2368, with the city or township assessor. Filing by June 1 lowers the summer levy, and a filing between June 2 and November 1 starts with the winter levy (Treasury PRE claim requirements).

At sale you have to undo it. Once the home is no longer your principal residence, send Form 2602, a Request to Rescind, to the assessor within 90 days. A late filing costs $5 a day, capped at $200, and the exemption comes off the roll at the end of the filing year.

The same duty reaches other situations. After an owner dies, the personal representative or trustee files it. After a divorce, the departing spouse files it. After a lender forecloses, the former borrower files it once the home is vacated. Closing agents, assessors and the Treasury website all hand out the forms.

Due dates and penalties

Township and city treasurers send the bills and collect first. A summer levy is a lien and is due July 1, and interest runs on anything collected after September 14. Whatever is still unpaid on March 1 goes to the county as delinquent (MCL 211.44a).

A collecting unit may add an administration fee of up to 1 percent to a bill paid before mid-February. From February 15 until the delinquent return, the city or township may authorize that fee plus a 3 percent late charge (MCL 211.44).

The serious step comes a year later. Each March 1, parcels that were delinquent for a full prior 12 months forfeit to the county treasurer, and a $175 fee is added. A certificate is recorded at the deeds office within 45 days. To redeem, you pay everything owed plus extra interest of one-half percent a month. Redemption stays open through the March 31 that follows the foreclosure judgment, or 21 days after judgment if the case is contested (MCL 211.78g). A seller with back taxes should ask the county treasurer for a written payoff figure well before then.

Seller checklist before closing

Start with the parcel's tax history and work outward. Closing agents ask for these same items, and a gap is cheaper to close early.

  • Ask the township or city treasurer which bills are paid, then ask the county office whether any year went delinquent.
  • Check the exemption status with the assessor, and send in the rescission form within 90 days of moving out.
  • Tell the buyer that taxable value moves up to SEV the year after closing, so last year's bill understates what comes next.
  • To contest the assessment on a house, plan for the March board first and the July 31 tribunal date after it.
  • For an inherited house, find out whether the family exception keeps the old taxable value before the heirs decide whether to keep or sell.

Owners several years behind should act before forfeiture. After it, the parcel sits with the county treasurer, and the foreclosing governmental unit takes possession only on the April 1 after judgment. Redemption ends at the March 31 cutoff.

What a cash sale changes

Back taxes, a lingering exemption or a pending appeal can slow a traditional listing, because a buyer's lender and title company want clean numbers. In a cash sale, a buyer who pays from their own funds does not wait on a lender's underwriting, so the tax payoff can be settled at closing from the proceeds. You still need the written payoff figure from the treasurer, and you still file the rescission form after you move. What a cash sale skips is the repair list, the appraisal and the lender's timeline.

If you are weighing an offer while taxes are owed, line up three things first: the payoff letter, the parcel number from your tax bill, and the date you stopped living in the home. With those in hand the closing agent can show exactly what comes out of the proceeds and what the buyer takes on.

Frequently asked questions

When does the Michigan board of review meet?

The week of the second Monday in March. Some cities and townships open one or two days later, on the Tuesday or Wednesday, and every board owes 12 hours of hearings that week, with three after 6 p.m.

When must a homeowner petition the Michigan Tax Tribunal?

Your petition must be filed by July 31 of the tax year. Residential cases generally begin with a board of review protest. Commercial and industrial real property follow an earlier May 31 date.

Do Michigan property taxes go up when a house is sold?

Often. A transfer of ownership sets taxable value equal to SEV for the next calendar year, wiping out the Proposal A gap the seller built up. The buyer reports the transfer to the assessor within 45 days.

How do I remove the principal residence exemption after selling?

Send Form 2602 to the local assessor within 90 days of ceasing to live there as your principal residence. Missing the window triggers $5 per day, with a $200 ceiling.

When does Michigan property go into forfeiture for unpaid taxes?

Each March 1, after taxes have gone unpaid for the prior 12 months or longer. The parcel is forfeited to the county treasurer for the amount owed, and redemption by full payment stays possible through the following March 31 after the foreclosure judgment.

Michigan Principal Residence Exemption: Who Qualifies and When to File

Michigan's principal residence exemption

It's a break on the school operating part of your property tax bill. The exemption removes the local school operating millage, up to 18 mills, from the bill of an owner's principal residence. The statute behind it is MCL 211.7cc.

People often call it the homestead exemption, but Michigan keeps two ideas apart. The Homestead Property Tax Credit is a separate credit claimed on an income tax return. The exemption covered here is claimed with the local assessor and shows up on the tax roll.

A principal residence is the one place where an owner has a true, fixed and permanent home to which the owner intends to return whenever absent. It also reaches unoccupied residential or timber-cutover land next to the dwelling that the owner owns and occupies (MCL 211.7dd(c)).

Who counts as an owner

Only an individual with a documented ownership interest. Verbal agreements create no interest, and the person claiming carries the burden of proof. These owners are eligible:

  • A person who owns the property, including a partial owner.
  • A land contract purchaser under a written contract that the seller signed.
  • A holder of a life estate, who is treated as a partial owner.
  • A beneficiary who receives ownership rights under a will, a trust, or intestate succession.
  • A grantor who placed the home in a revocable trust or a qualified personal residence trust.
  • A cooperative housing corporation or a registered life care facility.

An LLC, a corporation, a shareholder of a corporation, and a sole member of an LLC don't qualify. A trust isn't itself an owner, though its grantor or beneficiaries may be. A married couple filing a joint Michigan return gets only one exemption (MCL 211.7cc(3)).

Where and when to file the affidavit

File Form 2368, the Principal Residence Exemption Affidavit, with the assessor for the city or township where the home sits. The statute sets June 1 for the summer levy and November 1 for the winter levy (MCL 211.7cc(2)). A valid affidavit filed by June 1 reduces that year's bill starting with the summer levy. One filed from June 2 through November 1 reduces it starting with the winter levy.

The affidavit swears that you own and occupy the property on the signing date and haven't claimed a substantially similar break in another state. Claiming both brings a $500 penalty. A false claim can also bring perjury charges, with penalties that include up to a year in jail and fines of $1,000 to $5,000 (MCL 211.120).

Closing agents and local assessors hand out the forms, and Treasury posts them too. A closing statement preparer who skips the forms isn't legally liable for that, so the seller and buyer should ask for them.

If you missed a deadline

You can still file. File Form 2368 with the local assessor at any time during the year. The assessor may grant the exemption back through the current year and the three years before it, provided you met the requirements on June 1 or November 1 of each year claimed. If the owner has died, the estate can file for the same period.

The July and December Boards of Review no longer have authority to grant late claims. Only the assessor does, so go to the assessor's office instead of waiting for a board hearing.

Dates and rules at a glance

Principal residence exemption timing rules
EventRuleStatute
Claim for summer levyAffidavit on or before June 1MCL 211.7cc(2)
Claim for winter levyAffidavit on or before November 1MCL 211.7cc(2)
Home stops being principal residenceRescind within 90 days using Form 2602MCL 211.7cc(5)

Rescission takes effectRemoved as of December 31 of the filing yearMCL 211.7cc(15)
Appeal of a denial35 days to the Michigan tax tribunalMCL 211.7cc(13)

Two parcels, a duplex or a split lot

Each parcel needs its own affidavit. If your home sits on one parcel and contiguous residential land is a second parcel, both need Form 2368. When a parcel is split or combined, the new parcel numbers call for a fresh affidavit.

If the home is one unit of a multiple-unit dwelling, or a dwelling within a mixed-use building, you claim only the share of taxable value used as your principal residence, in the manner Treasury prescribes (MCL 211.7cc(16)). A landlord who lives in one side of a duplex therefore claims that side only. Ask the local assessor how the portion is measured before you file.

What a seller must do with the exemption

The exemption lasts until December 31 of the year the property is transferred, or until it stops being a principal residence (MCL 211.7cc(4)). Within 90 days after you stop using the home as your principal residence, file Form 2602 with the local tax collecting unit. Rescission is still required in several cases: the owner dies, a spouse leaves after a divorce, or the owner moves out during a foreclosure redemption period.

There's one holding option if you moved and the house is for sale. An owner who claims the exemption on a new current residence can keep it on the old home for up to 3 tax years by filing a conditional rescission form, as long as the old home is unoccupied, listed for sale, not leased, and not used for business. Lease it and the local unit denies the conditional rescission back to the prior December 31.

An owner who moved into a nursing home or assisted living facility may keep the exemption if the home stays owned, no new principal residence is set up, the home is maintained, and it isn't leased or used for business.

Denials, audits and back taxes

An assessor who believes the home isn't the owner's principal residence can deny a new or existing claim in writing, for the current year and up to the three years before. The owner has 35 days from the notice date to appeal to the residential and small claims division of the Michigan tax tribunal, and doesn't have to pay the disputed tax to appeal. Counties can elect to audit claims, and Treasury audits annually in counties that don't.

Back taxes carry interest at 1.25% per month or fraction of a month from the date they were last payable without penalty. If the home was sold to a bona fide purchaser before the extra bill went out, the tax, interest and penalties aren't a lien on the property and aren't billed to that buyer. Treasury assesses the former owner instead. That protection is one reason to rescind promptly.

A land contract buyer has one more filing: a Property Transfer Affidavit, Form 2766, with the local assessor within 45 days of the transfer.

Before you list: a seller's checklist

Run through this list a few weeks before you put the house on the market, or before you accept a cash offer.

  • Find out whether an affidavit is on file for each parcel you own.
  • Pick your move-out date and mark 90 days from it for Form 2602.
  • If you're buying another home first, ask the assessor about the conditional rescission for the house you're selling.
  • Give the buyer a copy of the transfer affidavit requirement so they can file within 45 days of the transfer.

A fast cash closing doesn't change these deadlines. The exemption still ends on December 31 of the year of transfer, and the buyer starts their own claim by filing Form 2368 once they own and occupy the home.

Frequently asked questions

Does Michigan's exemption cover the whole property tax bill?

No. It removes the local school operating millage, up to 18 mills. Other millages still apply, so a bill drops but doesn't vanish.

Can I claim it on a cottage with a higher taxable value than my house?

No. The exemption is only for the property that is your true, fixed and permanent home, never for the sake of potential tax savings.

Do I have to file a new affidavit every year?

No. A valid claim stays on the property while the owner keeps meeting the requirements. A new affidavit is needed when a parcel is split or combined, because that creates new parcel numbers.

Who files the rescission when an owner dies?

The estate's personal representative or trustee files Form 2602 with the assessor within 90 days of death, because the deceased owner can no longer occupy the home or intend to return.

What if my trust owns the house?

The grantor or beneficiary who lives there signs Form 2368 in their own name, with the trust role noted. If the grantor can't sign, the trustee may sign on the grantor's behalf.

Michigan transfer tax when a house sells

A deed given for money triggers two separate levies. Michigan takes $3.75 for each $500 step of value, and any leftover amount counts as a full step (MCL 207.525(1)). The county adds 55 cents on that same step where it has fewer than two million people. Only the largest counties may authorize more, up to 75 cents (MCL 207.504).

Together the ordinary pair comes to $8.60 on each $1,000 of price. The step rule bites at the edges: a price one dollar over a $500 line is taxed as if it had reached the next full step, which adds $4.30 at the ordinary rates. County charts print every bracket in turn for this reason.

Recording is the trigger. The deed or sale contract must display the total real property value, or carry an affidavit that does. When a sale bundles land with furnishings or equipment, only the real property is taxed, and only when the instrument lists the two values apart.

Rates at a glance

The two layers stack, and a title agent normally quotes the total before closing. Midland County and Monroe County both publish charts built on these same rates.

Michigan transfer tax rates on a deed given for money
LayerPer $500 of valuePer $1,000 of value
State tax$3.75$7.50
County tax, standard rate55 cents$1.10
County tax, largest countiesUp to 75 centsSet by the county
State plus standard county$4.30$8.60

To estimate your own bill, count the $500 steps in the sale price, rounding a partial step up, and multiply by the combined rate for your county. Your closing agent will confirm the final figure on the settlement statement.

Who pays at the closing table

The seller, called the grantor in the statute, owes the state tax. That is the plain text of MCL 207.523(2). Subsection (3) gives fifteen days from the day the deed reaches the buyer, with payment going to the treasurer in whichever county holds the parcel. Closing agents usually withhold the amount from the seller's proceeds.

A purchase agreement may assign the cost to the buyer instead. Whoever paid can request a refund from the Department of Treasury when the sale turns out to have qualified for an exemption, and subsection (4) reaches back four years. Read the cost clause in your contract and ask for an itemized settlement statement before you sign.

Sales that escape the state tax

Section 6 of the state act, MCL 207.526, runs through nearly two dozen exemptions. These come up most for homeowners:

  • A deed where the stated consideration is below $100.
  • A family deed handed down to a son, daughter, stepchild, adopted child or grandchild.
  • A quitclaim or other corrective deed that merely confirms title already vested in the grantee.
  • A foreclosure transfer or deed in lieu, with the lender's own resale taxed later.
  • A court judgment or order that sets no price.
  • A land contract that keeps legal title with the seller until the price is paid in full.
  • A deed forming a joint tenancy in which at least one joint owner already held the property.

Leases, security instruments, and spousal deeds that make or end a tenancy by the entireties also fall outside the tax.

Does the county tax follow the same list?

The county act is shorter. MCL 207.505 covers papers under $100, leases, security instruments, personal property interests, price-free court orders, boundary line fixes, title confirmations, qualifying land contracts, mineral rights and certain joint tenancies. It has no line for a deed to a child or grandchild and no general foreclosure exemption, though it does exempt foreclosures on government-backed loans.

A parent planning to deed a house to a daughter or son for token money should phone the county's recording office first and describe the exact deed.

Does the deed have to show the price?

Not always. Under MCL 207.525(2), an affidavit of total value can replace the printed price, using a form that Treasury prescribes. Midland County's recording office accepts a Real Estate Transfer Tax Valuation Affidavit so the figure can stay off the deed.

Both routes still produce a number for the tax math, and that number later reaches the assessor on the buyer's transfer affidavit. The deed, the affidavit and the settlement statement should all agree.

Land contract sales

Neither transfer tax reaches a land contract while legal title stays with the seller. Property tax law sees it differently. MCL 211.27a(6)(b) treats the contract itself as a transfer of ownership, so taxable value resets the calendar year after signing and stays put when the deed finally records.

If the contract carries a warranty clause, ask the treasurer's office for a tax certificate, because recording requires one.

Tax certificates and recording costs

The recording side is small next to the tax. A warranty deed needs a tax certificate from the treasurer, which costs $5 for up to five legal descriptions in both Midland County and Monroe County. Beyond five, Midland adds $1.00 per description and Monroe adds $0.20.

The tax certificate and the transfer tax both go to the treasurer, so a seller with several parcels, such as a house plus an adjoining lot, should line up the descriptions early. Each extra description changes the certificate cost, and the combined value still sets the transfer tax.

MCL 600.2567 sets the recording charge at $30 per document, with no page count. Five dollars of it is routed to the automation fund. Documents that assign or discharge several instruments add $3 per extra, a plain copy runs $1 a page, and certifying one costs $5. Charter counties can adopt their own schedules by ordinance, so verify the figure locally.

After closing

Once the sale closes, the buyer has 45 days to send the local assessor the notice described in MCL 211.27a(10). That filing is the buyer's job, but a seller who mentions it at the closing table saves everyone a follow-up call.

Before the closing date, a seller can do four things to keep the tax line on the settlement statement from surprising anyone:

  • Read the purchase agreement to see whether the seller or the buyer is assigned the transfer tax.
  • Ask the title agent for the county's current rate, since only the largest counties may charge more than the standard one.
  • Decide whether the deed will state the price or carry a value affidavit, and use the same total on every document.
  • Check the exemption list above if the deed goes to a family member or only confirms existing title.

In a cash sale the same tax applies, and the same closing agent collects it from the proceeds. What a cash sale skips is the lender's timeline, so the tax figure can be settled early and the deed recorded soon after funds move.

Frequently asked questions

Which rate does the state apply?

$3.75 for each $500 of value, rounded up for a partial step. That is $7.50 per $1,000 of price, set by MCL 207.525(1).

What does a typical county charge?

A county with fewer than two million people charges 55 cents per $500, or $1.10 per $1,000. A larger county may authorize up to 75 cents under MCL 207.504.

Is a deed from a parent to a child taxed?

The state tax exempts a conveyance from an individual to a child, stepchild, adopted child or grandchild under MCL 207.526(j) and (k). The county act has no matching entry, so confirm with the county's recording office before relying on it.

Do foreclosure deeds carry the tax?

The state act exempts a deed given in foreclosure or in lieu of foreclosure, though a later resale by the foreclosing entity is taxed. The county act is narrower, so confirm locally.

What is the flat recording charge for a deed?

$30 per document under MCL 600.2567, whatever the page count. Charter counties may set a different schedule, and each extra instrument assigned or discharged adds $3.

How an eviction starts in Michigan

No Michigan landlord may remove a tenant without the court. The landlord serves a written notice, waits out the notice period, and then files a summary proceeding in district court. For unpaid rent the notice is a written demand for possession, and the tenant has 7 days from service to pay or leave (MCL 600.5714(1)(a)).

The statute sets short clocks for these cases, counted in days. An owner planning a sale feels them directly, since the court calendar decides when the keys can change hands.

The landlord-tenant statute states the rent rule too: when a tenant neglects or refuses to pay rent, the landlord may end the tenancy with a written 7-day notice to quit (MCL 554.134(2)).

Notices that come before a case is filed

Each notice ties to a different reason for ending the tenancy. The notice has to match the ground the landlord relies on, so sending the wrong one can cost time.

  • Unpaid rent: a written demand for possession, 7 days to pay or leave.
  • Controlled substance clause: a 24-hour written demand, but only where a formal police report has been filed.
  • Threat or injury to a person on the landlord's property: a 7-day written notice to quit, again tied to a police notification.
  • Serious health hazard or extensive damage discovered within 90 days before filing: a 7-day demand to hand back possession or repair.
  • Tenancy at will or by sufferance: one month's notice, or a notice equal to the rent interval if rent is paid more often than every 3 months.
  • Year-to-year tenancy: a notice to quit that ends the lease one year after service.

These grounds come from MCL 600.5714 and MCL 554.134. A tenant who stays after a lease ends under its own terms or by law also falls under summary proceedings.

How to deliver a rent demand

There are four accepted ways: hand it to the tenant, give it to a household member old enough to accept it, mail it by first class mail, or send it by email when the tenant agreed in writing and replied to a confirming message. The demand must describe the rental, state the rent owed, say the tenant has seven days, and show the landlord's address and the notice date.

Taping a notice to the door, sliding it under the door, or mailing it by a method that needs a signature are examples of improper service. If service was done wrong, restart the clock with a fresh demand before you file anything.

What happens once the landlord files

After filing, the court issues a summons. Under the standard rule in MCL 600.5735, trial is set within 10 days of issuance and the summons must be served at least 3 days before trial. A court may adopt a local rule that sets appearance 5 days after service instead. The hearing is to happen within 7 days after the appearance or trial date, and it can be pushed back further only by stipulation of the parties or on the record.

For unpaid rent the landlord has to show three things: the rent wasn't paid, a proper demand was served, and the tenant neither paid nor left within the seven days. A tenant may answer that the rent was paid, ask for a rent reduction for poor repair, or file a counterclaim for repair costs.

A tenant can also apply for rental assistance before the first court date or within 5 days after it. With proof of the application filed and served, the case is paused for 14 days and can be extended once for another 14. If you're selling, allow up to four extra weeks when assistance is pending.

Removal after judgment

Usually the writ waits 10 days after the judgment for possession. That is the default under MCL 600.5744(5), and it matches the 10 days a tenant gets to pay or move out after a rent judgment.

The statute carves out faster paths. A writ can issue right after judgment, on conditions the court sets, when a unit was ordered vacated for lacking a required certificate of compliance, when entry was forcible or possession is held by force, when the occupant is a trespasser, when a serious health hazard or continuing damage is proven, or in the controlled substance case.

Slower paths exist too. After a land contract forfeiture, no writ issues for 90 days if less than half the price was paid, or for 6 months if half or more was paid. In rent cases, paying the judgment amount and taxed costs inside the window stops the writ. When the writ is carried out, the officer removes occupants and belongings and either leaves the belongings in an area open to the public or delivers them to the sheriff.

Can an owner change the locks or cut utilities to speed things up?

No. MCL 600.2918 makes it unlawful for an owner to interfere with a tenant's possession by force or threat, by removing or keeping the tenant's belongings, by changing locks without handing over keys, by boarding up, by removing doors or windows, or by shutting off heat, water, or electric service the landlord must supply.

A tenant who proves interference can recover actual damages or $200, whichever is greater, for each occurrence, and can recover possession if it was lost. A person forced out in a forcible and unlawful manner can recover three times actual damages or $200, whichever is greater. These rights can't be waived in a lease.

The owner is protected when acting under a court order, when making needed repairs or inspections as the law allows, or when in good faith believing the tenant has abandoned the home after diligent inquiry and with current rent unpaid. Suits to regain possession must start within 90 days, and damage claims within one year.

Selling a rented house

The security deposit stays your problem after the sale. Under MCL 554.614, a landlord whose interest ends by sale stays liable for the deposit until it is passed to the successor with written notice to the tenant by ordinary mail, until the successor meets the deposit rules, or until the tenant gets it back. Settle it in the closing papers and keep proof of the mailing.

The statute also lets a new owner recover possession by summary proceedings in two sale-related cases: occupants who stay after a mortgage or execution sale once the redemption time has run, and occupants who stay after a personal representative sells under probate court license or will authority (MCL 600.5714(1)(g) and (h)). Beyond those, whether a lease survives a sale depends on the lease text and the notices already served. Check with the clerk of the district court that covers the property, or with a Michigan attorney, before a buyer is told the house will be vacant.

  • Gather the lease, rent ledger, deposit amount, and any notice already served.
  • Pick the notice only after you know which ground applies.
  • Tell the buyer up front whether the house comes occupied or empty.

Frequently asked questions

Is a 7-day notice enough to evict for unpaid rent in Michigan?

It starts the process but doesn't end it. After the 7 days run, the landlord must file in district court, win a judgment for possession, and wait for a writ, which normally can't issue until 10 days after judgment (MCL 600.5744(5)).

Can I end a tenancy at will so I can sell?

Yes, through a notice to quit and then summary proceedings if the tenant stays. A tenancy at will or by sufferance ends on one month's notice, or a period equal to the rent interval when rent is paid more often than every 3 months (MCL 554.134(1)).

Does paying the judgment stop the eviction?

For rent cases, yes, if the full judgment amount and taxed costs are paid to the landlord within the time provided. A writ of restitution can't issue after that payment (MCL 600.5744(7)).

What if the tenant applies for rental assistance?

The case is paused for 14 days when proof of the application is filed and served, and the pause can be extended for 14 more days with a status update. This applies to nonpayment cases.

Who gets the security deposit when the landlord sells?

The seller stays liable until the deposit reaches the buyer and the tenant is told by ordinary mail who the new landlord is and where to write, or until the tenant is repaid (MCL 554.614).

What makes a Michigan quitclaim deed valid

A deed worded in substance as "A.B. quit claims to C.D.", with the premises described and the consideration stated, is a good and sufficient quitclaim conveyance once the grantor signs, seals and acknowledges it. That rule is in MCL 565.152, part of a statute dating to 1881.

The statutory wording is short on purpose. A quitclaim passes whatever interest the grantor holds and promises nothing more, so it fits a transfer between people who already know the title, such as a spouse, a parent, or a co-owner buying out a sibling.

The form also leaves the price visible. Whatever consideration the deed recites feeds the transfer tax, the assessor's records and any later title review. Write the real figure, and use the same number on every document you sign.

Names matter more than people expect. Spell every grantor exactly as the prior deed does, and list each grantee's mailing address, because the recording statute rejects a deed whose printed names disagree with the acknowledgment.

A signed deed is only the start. It still has to meet the recording rules, and the transfer may bring a tax filing, a transfer tax question and a change in the property tax bill.

Formatting rules for recording

A deed that misses any item in the recording statute is refused for recording. The statute is MCL 565.201. Instruments executed after April 1, 1997 face the most detailed checklist:

  • A legible printed name under every signature, in black or navy ink, matching the name in the acknowledgment.
  • The grantee's address on the deed, with a street number where street numbers are in common use.
  • The name of whoever prepared the document, with that person's business address.
  • One line of text at the top that names the recordable event, such as the type of deed.
  • Blank space of 2-1/2 inches across the head of the first sheet, with half-inch margins on all other sides.
  • Print in 10-point type or bigger, dark ink, on white stock weighing no less than 20 pounds, sized from letter up to legal length.
  • Any Social Security number blacked out except its last four digits.
  • An English translation attached if any part is in another language.

The notary's printed name belongs beside the notary's signature on that same sheet. Run your draft against this list before driving to the county seat, because a rejected deed means a second trip.

Does a quitclaim deed carry Michigan transfer tax?

Often it does, because the tax applies to deeds given for consideration. The seller or grantor owes it, and payment is due at the county treasurer's office no later than 15 days from the handover of the deed (MCL 207.523).

Two layers apply. State tax runs $3.75 per $500 block of value, rounded up for any partial block (MCL 207.525). The county levy is 55 cents a block where the population is under 2,000,000, and a county above that size may authorize up to 75 cents (MCL 207.504). Either the deed itself states the full value being transferred, or a value affidavit travels with it. When real and personal property are sold together, only the land and buildings are taxed if the values are shown separately.

Ask the treasurer's office or the recording office which value affidavit to attach, and which of the two collects the tax at the counter in your county.

Quitclaim deeds that escape transfer tax

The state act lists the exemptions in MCL 207.526, and the county act in MCL 207.505 has a shorter list. These are the ones that matter most for quitclaim deeds.

Common transfer tax exemptions for deeds in Michigan
SituationExempt from transfer tax?
Re-confirming title the grantee already holds, such as correcting a defectYes, state and county
Individual conveying to a son, daughter, stepchild or adopted childYes, state tax
Individual conveying to a grandchild, step-grandchild or adopted grandchildYes, state tax
Spouses creating or ending an entireties tenancyYes, state and county
New joint tenancy where one of the joint owners already owned the landYes, state and county
Consideration under $100Yes, state and county

If the tax was paid and the transfer later turns out to have qualified, the seller, or a buyer who paid on the seller's behalf, may ask Treasury for a refund in the form and manner it sets. The statute reaches back four years for transfers that qualify.

Recording the deed and the fee

Bring the signed deed to the recording office serving the parcel's county. Under MCL 600.2567 the office charges a flat $30 to enter and record a document, regardless of length. Certifying a recorded document adds $5, and plain copies run $1.00 a page. A charter county may set its own schedule, so confirm the amount before you go.

Where the register accepts electronic recording under the Uniform Real Property Electronic Recording Act, payment is expected a business day after the file is received, which is a different clock from the counter rule.

Recording protects the new owner. An unrecorded conveyance loses to a later good-faith purchaser who gave value and got a deed on the record first. A first recorded deed that happens to be a quitclaim does not by itself put that purchaser on notice of the earlier one (MCL 565.29).

How a quitclaim deed affects the property tax bill

A deed is a transfer of ownership under MCL 211.27a, and the grantee owes the local assessing office a notice within 45 days. In the following calendar year, taxable value normally jumps to the state equalized figure.

Transfers of residential property to the transferor's or spouse's parent, child, brother, sister or grandchild are excluded from the definition, provided the home is not put to commercial use afterward. A transfer between spouses is excluded too. Still, confirm the filing with the assessor, because a missing filing on a taxable transfer carries a $5 daily penalty with a $200 cap for a principal residence, plus back taxes. Our page on the Michigan Property Transfer Affidavit walks through the deadline and penalties.

When a quitclaim deed is the wrong tool for a sale

The statutory form names a grantor, a grantee, the premises and the consideration. It contains no promise about what interest the grantor actually holds, so the form alone tells a buyer nothing about liens, missed heirs or unpaid taxes.

That gap matters in a sale at market price. Before signing, find out what is already recorded against the parcel and whether any taxes are unpaid. Have a Michigan attorney review any transfer that involves a loan, a divorce, an estate or more than one co-owner, because the deed does not change the loan agreement or settle who else claims an interest.

If you plan to sell for cash, expect the buyer's title company to ask the same questions. Gather the prior deed, the parcel number and any payoff letters first, and the closing goes faster. A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and underwriting, but it does not skip the title search or the recording step.

Frequently asked questions

Which office records a Michigan quitclaim deed?

The register of deeds serving the parcel. A charter county may set its own fee schedule, and the default under MCL 600.2567 is $30 a document.

Is a quitclaim deed to my child exempt from transfer tax?

The state transfer tax exempts a conveyance from an individual to that individual's child, stepchild or adopted child (MCL 207.526(j)). Grandchildren are covered by subsection (k). Ask the county treasurer how the county tax exemption is claimed.

What happens if I never record the deed?

It becomes void against a later good-faith buyer who pays value and records first (MCL 565.29). Record soon after signing.

How soon must the transfer tax be paid?

Fifteen days from handover of the deed, paid to the parcel's county treasurer. The grantor carries the liability.

Does the new owner have to tell the assessor?

Yes, in most cases. The grantee must notify the local assessing office within 45 days of a transfer of ownership, and excluded transfers such as those between spouses are still worth raising with the assessor.

Michigan taxes a home sale gain like ordinary income

Michigan has no separate capital gains schedule. Profit on a house goes into the same state income tax that applies to wages and other income. For the 2026 tax year the state rate is a flat 4.25 percent, set by Michigan Treasury in an April 15, 2026 announcement after its yearly review.

So whatever part of your gain is taxable lands on your Michigan return at that single rate. Ask Treasury or a tax preparer how the federal exclusion carries onto the MI-1040 for your sale.

A formula in state law drives the rate. Treasury and the two legislative fiscal agencies run it after each year's financial report comes out. General fund revenue fell 1.56 percent in the fiscal year ended September 30, 2025 while inflation ran 2.70 percent, so no reduction was triggered. A 2024 court decision held that any cut the formula triggers lasts only one year.

How much gain you can exclude

IRS Topic 701 lets a single seller exclude up to $250,000 of gain on a main home. A married couple filing together can exclude up to $500,000. Run this exclusion first, before you estimate any state tax.

Two tests apply, both measured over the five years ending on the closing date:

  • Ownership: you or your spouse held title for 24 months or more.
  • Use: the house was your residence for 24 months or longer. On a joint return each spouse has to meet this one personally.
  • Look-back limit: a sale in the prior two years that already used the exclusion usually blocks a second claim.

The two 24-month periods don't have to be the same stretch. Each just has to fall inside that five-year window. IRS Publication 523 has the full rules, the worksheets and the exceptions to the two-year requirement.

What to report on your returns

If the closing agent files a Form 1099-S, you must put the sale on your return, even when the exclusion wipes out every dollar of gain. A gain above the exclusion has to be reported too.

  • Use Schedule D and Form 8949 when the sale is reportable.
  • If the buyer pays you over several years, the deal is an installment sale and is reported by the installment method unless you elect out. The exclusion still applies.
  • Uniformed Services, Foreign Service and intelligence community staff on qualified extended duty can pause the five-year clock for as long as a decade.

On the Michigan side, Treasury's tax year 2025 guidance sets a senior interest, dividend and capital gain limit of $14,688 for single filers and $29,376 for joint filers. Whether you qualify depends on your age and filing details, so read the current MI-1040 instructions or call Treasury before you count on it for a home sale.

Deed taxes are separate from income tax

Michigan also charges a state deed tax (MCL 207.525) and a county deed tax (MCL 207.504). They attach to the deed and ignore your profit. Both statutes name the seller as the party who owes them.

Income tax follows the gain. Deed tax follows the sale price. If you bought at $180,000 and sold at $230,000, the deed tax is figured on the full price even when the whole gain is excluded. Our Michigan closing costs page covers the deed taxes and recording fee in detail.

Amending a return that left out a home sale

A taxpayer has 4 years from the due date of the original return to file and claim a refund with Michigan Treasury. Treasury's own example: a 2021 return and any homestead property tax credit claim had to be filed on or before April 18, 2026.

That window cuts both ways. If you sold in an earlier year, left the sale off and later learned part of the gain was excludable, you have limited time to claim a refund. If you owe tax, don't wait for the window to close. Michigan Treasury eServices handles free filing of the state return, online payments, refund status checks and replies to Treasury letters in one place.

Treasury's tax year 2025 guidance also sets the Michigan homestead property tax credit at a maximum taxable value of $165,400 and a credit limit of $1,900. If you sold partway through a year, call Treasury about how that affects a claim.

Inherited, rented or short-term homes

The two-year tests settle most of these cases. A house you inherited and never lived in fails the use test, so the main home exclusion generally won't apply to its sale. A house you lived in for only part of your ownership can still pass if you used it as your residence for 24 months inside the last five years.

For inherited property, a recipient's basis in certain property from a decedent has to match the value finally set for federal estate tax purposes. That rule comes from Internal Revenue Code sections 6035 and 1014(f) and applies when the estate had to file an estate tax return. Ask the estate's personal representative whether a Form 8971 statement was issued to you.

If you rented the property for part of the time, talk to a tax preparer about depreciation and how the use test applies. Publication 523 covers those cases, and Michigan Treasury answers state filing questions.

Before you list: a short checklist

Gather these before you talk numbers with a buyer or a tax preparer. They decide whether you owe anything at all.

  • The date you bought and the date you moved in, to count the 24-month ownership and use periods.
  • Your purchase price, closing statement and records of improvements, to work out your gain.
  • Whether either spouse already used the exclusion on a sale in the last two years.
  • Any Form 8971 statement if the house came from an estate.

A cash sale does not change any of this. The tax rules follow your gain and your years in the house, not how the buyer pays or how fast the sale closes. What a cash sale does skip is the wait for a buyer's lender, so the closing statement and any 1099-S usually arrive sooner.

Frequently asked questions

Does Michigan have a separate capital gains tax?

No. A home sale gain is taxed at the state's single individual rate, set at 4.25 percent for 2026. No extra state schedule exists for real estate gains.

Is the federal home sale exclusion honored in Michigan?

The exclusion is a federal rule and Michigan Treasury sets the state return. Read the current MI-1040 instructions or call Treasury to see how an excluded gain is entered.

Do I owe Michigan tax after living in the house under two years?

Possibly. The federal exclusion wants 24 months of ownership and 24 months of use in the last five years. IRS Publication 523 lists exceptions to the two-year rule.

Will I receive a 1099-S after closing a Michigan sale?

Often, yes. A seller who receives that form must report the sale on a return, even if the gain is entirely excludable. Ask the closing agent whether one will be filed for yours.

Does the buyer pay the Michigan transfer tax?

The statute names the seller as the one who owes it. A purchase contract can shift the cost, so read the closing statement before you sign.

What a Michigan land contract is and why it matters at sale

A Michigan land contract is an installment sale. The buyer (the vendee) pays the seller (the vendor) over time and takes possession now, while the vendor keeps legal title until the contract is paid. Because title stays split from possession, a house under a land contract can't be sold the way an ordinary owner-occupied home is, and every move depends on which side of the contract you're on.

The contract's own wording drives most outcomes. State law adds a few fixed rules about forfeiture, court timelines, taxes and recording. They come from the Revised Judicature Act, the Land Contracts act and the General Property Tax Act, all posted on the Michigan Legislature website.

  • A vendor who wants out can sell the right to future payments, pay off the buyer's side, or take the property back through forfeiture or foreclosure.
  • A vendee who wants out can assign the contract, pay it off with new financing and take a deed, or hand the property back.
  • A third-party buyer, including one paying cash, must learn who holds title and what is owed before offering anything.

How a vendor forfeits a land contract

A vendor can recover possession by summary proceedings only when the contract itself provides for termination or forfeiture after nonpayment or another material breach (MCL 600.5726). If the contract is silent on forfeiture, that route is closed. Accelerated indebtedness doesn't count as money required to be paid, so a vendor can't declare the whole balance due and then forfeit over it.

Before any court filing, the vendee must be served with a written notice of forfeiture (MCL 600.5728). The notice has to name the parties, give the contract date and the address or legal description, list the unpaid amounts with their due dates, and list any other material breaches. The vendor, an attorney or an agent must date and sign it.

The vendee then has 15 days to pay what is owed and cure other breaches, unless the parties agreed in writing to a longer period. If the vendee does neither, the vendor may file for possession in court.

How long a vendee can stay after a possession order

The wait depends on how much of the price has been paid. Under MCL 600.5744(4), a writ of restitution after a forfeiture judgment can't issue until 90 days have gone by if less than half the purchase price is paid, or six months if half or more is paid.

A vendee can still stop the process by paying the judgment amount plus taxed costs, and by curing any other material breach, within that window. Once a writ does issue, the vendee's equitable right of redemption is cut off. That makes the writ date the real deadline for anyone trying to save the contract or sell their interest.

  • Under half paid: 90 days after the judgment before a writ can issue.
  • Half or more paid: six months after the judgment.
  • Payment of the judgment sum and costs, plus cure of other breaches, blocks the writ.

Unpaid money after a forfeiture judgment

Forfeiture is a trade: the vendor gets the property back and gives up the money claim. MCL 600.5750 says a judgment for possession after forfeiture merges and bars any claim for payments due or in arrears at the time of trial. If a writ of restitution issues, claims for payments that would have come due later are barred as well.

The vendor keeps a separate right to damages from the time of the notice of forfeiture. For payments the vendee already made, the contract and the court decide, so ask a Michigan attorney how your contract treats them.

Vendors who would rather collect the debt than recover the house can ask the circuit court to foreclose the land contract, since the circuit court has jurisdiction to foreclose mortgages and land contracts under MCL 600.3101. Any surplus from a sale under a foreclosure judgment goes to the court for the defendant or whoever is entitled to it (MCL 600.3135).

Borrowing against a land contract interest

Either side can. The Land Contracts act lets a vendor or a vendee grant a land contract mortgage to secure any debt that a real estate mortgage could secure (MCL 565.357). It treats the vendor's right to payments and the vendee's right to a conveyance as real property interests. Any contract clause that bars or defaults a mortgage, sale or assignment stays in force, so a due-on-sale style clause still counts.

A land contract mortgage is signed, acknowledged and recorded the same way as a real estate mortgage, and a recorded one is perfected without a separate commercial-code filing (MCL 565.358). For a seller this means a title search on a contract property may show liens against either party's interest, not just against the vendor's deed.

Taxes and recording on a land contract sale

For property tax, the General Property Tax Act treats a land contract as a transfer of ownership. Under MCL 211.27a(6)(b), taxable value is reset to the state equalized value for the year after the contract is signed, and it isn't reset a second time when the deed is later recorded. The buyer has to notify the local assessor of the transfer within 45 days on the State Tax Commission form.

For the state transfer tax, MCL 207.526(o) exempts a land contract in which legal title doesn't pass until the full price is paid. The deed given at payoff is a separate document, so ask the register of deeds in the county what is due at that stage.

How to sell a house under a land contract

Start by pulling the signed contract, the payment history and any recorded memorandum or mortgage from the register of deeds in the county where the house sits. Those papers tell you who can convey what, how much is still owed, and whether a default is already on the clock.

  • Vendors: confirm whether the vendee is current, whether the contract allows forfeiture, and whether a payoff or a negotiated assignment is faster than a court case.
  • Vendees: ask the vendor in writing for a payoff figure, and check the contract for limits on assigning your interest before you market the property.
  • Heirs of either party: the person's interest in the contract passes to devisees or heirs subject to estate administration, so the probate rules apply before anyone signs a deed.
  • Buyers: expect the closing to include a payoff to the vendor, release of any land contract mortgage, and a deed from whoever holds record title.

A forfeiture case narrows the time available. A vendee, or a buyer stepping into the vendee's position, who pays the judgment sum and costs and cures other breaches inside the 90-day or six-month window stops the writ and keeps the contract alive.

What happens at closing on a contract payoff

A payoff closing looks a lot like an ordinary one, with the vendor playing the part of the lender. The vendee brings new financing or cash, the vendor is paid the remaining balance, and the vendor signs a deed that moves legal title to the vendee or to a new buyer.

  • Get a written payoff figure from the vendor before the closing date.
  • Have the title company confirm any land contract mortgage is released.
  • Record the deed and file the assessor notice inside the 45-day window.

A cash buyer can shorten this, because no lender's underwriting sits between the payoff and the deed. The contract still has to be current or cured, so a default must be settled before the title company will close.

Frequently asked questions

How many days does a Michigan land contract buyer get to cure after a forfeiture notice?

Fifteen days, unless the parties agreed in writing to a longer period. The 15 days run from service of the written notice, and the notice must itself declare forfeiture effective at the end of that period.

Can a vendor forfeit a land contract if the contract never mentions forfeiture?

No. MCL 600.5726 allows summary proceedings only when the contract expressly provides for termination or forfeiture, or gives the vendor the right to declare one, after nonpayment or another material breach.

How long before a writ of restitution issues after a land contract judgment?

It depends on payments made. A writ can't issue until 90 days after judgment if less than 50 percent of the price is paid, or six months after judgment if 50 percent or more is paid. Paying the judgment amount and costs and curing other breaches inside that time blocks the writ.

Does a land contract change the property tax on a Michigan house?

It can. A land contract counts as a transfer of ownership, so the taxable value is reset to the state equalized value for the following year. The buyer must notify the local assessor within 45 days of the transfer.

Can a land contract buyer sell the house before paying it off?

Often yes, but the contract controls. Check for clauses limiting assignment or sale, get a written payoff from the vendor, and make sure the vendor's title and any land contract mortgage are cleared at closing so the new buyer receives a deed.

Michigan's inheritance tax is limited to old estates

Michigan Treasury says the inheritance tax remains in effect only for people who inherited from someone who died on or before September 30, 1993. If the person whose house you're selling died after that date, the Michigan inheritance tax doesn't apply to what you received.

An inheritance tax is a tax on the right to receive property. That separates it from an estate tax, which is charged on the estate itself before assets are handed out.

When an old estate can still owe

Treasury describes three situations in which an old estate can still need a tax determination. In each one the sender must write to Treasury within 90 days of the triggering event.

  • Estate reopened for a later-found asset: a probate estate is reopened because an asset turned up after the estate closed. Treasury wants the discovery date, the type of asset and its date-of-death value.
  • First-time probate where an asset appears: the letter gives the same facts, plus the petition to commence proceedings and the probate inventory.
  • Trust with deferred tax: when a life beneficiary dies and the trustee must make final distributions, the trustee reports the beneficiary's date of death and a breakdown of the remaining beneficiaries and their relationship to the original decedent.

If the asset is real estate, Treasury also asks for a statement from the local community showing the state equalized value as close to the date of death as possible. Include the will or trust agreement with every letter.

Where to send inheritance tax questions

Write to the Michigan Department of Treasury, Inheritance Tax Section, Austin Building, 430 W Allegan St., Lansing, MI 48922. The section's phone number is (517) 636-4419. Keep the letter factual and attach the documents Treasury names, since the section decides from the file.

Most sellers will never need this office. It matters only when the person who died did so on or before September 30, 1993, and a property or asset from that estate is still unresolved.

An estate that must file Form 706 also owes a statement on Form 8971 to the IRS and to each person who receives property. The statement lets a beneficiary match their basis to the value finally set for federal estate tax purposes. If the estate didn't have to file a return, the IRS asks that no Form 8971 be sent.

Property tax after inheriting a house

The reset doesn't happen when the heir is the decedent's spouse. Treasury or the assessor can ask for proof of the relationship, and the heir has 30 days to supply it or face a $200 fine.

The new owner also owes the local assessor a notice of the transfer within 45 days.

  • Local assessor: receives the 45-day transfer notice and can tell you whether the taxable value will reset for the buyer or for a family member who keeps the house.
  • Recording office: files the deed at $30 under MCL 600.2567 and passes each recorded transfer on to the assessor.

The probate court for the county controls whether a personal representative has authority to sell. Bring letters of authority to the first call so the offices can see who signs the deed.

Basis rules when an heir sells

The IRS issued final regulations on September 16, 2024 on consistent basis reporting between an estate and the person who acquires property from a decedent. They carry out a 2015 federal law that created Internal Revenue Code section 6035 and added section 1014(f).

Under section 6035 the executor of an estate that must file an estate tax return sends statements to the IRS and to each beneficiary. The heir's basis in covered property has to line up with the value finally set for estate tax. If you plan to sell, ask the executor for that statement early. The basis figure drives the gain on a later sale, as described on our capital gains page.

Does selling an inherited house trigger transfer tax?

Usually yes, because the personal representative is the seller or grantor and the deed is for consideration. The state and county deed taxes, $3.75 and $0.55 per $500 in most counties, are explained on our Michigan closing costs page.

Two exemptions in MCL 207.526 can change the outcome. One covers a deed to a son, daughter, stepchild or grandchild. The other covers a transfer made by court order where the court sets no dollar price. A deed to a child can therefore carry no state deed tax, while a sale on the open market is taxed.

MCL 600.5714(1)(h) also lets a buyer recover possession by summary proceedings if a person stays in a house sold and conveyed by a personal representative under probate court license or the authority of the will.

Is there a Michigan estate tax I have to pay on a house?

The inheritance tax applies only to deaths on or before September 30, 1993. For a later death, call Treasury or the probate court about state filings, and check the federal limit of $15,000,000 for 2026.

How large is the federal exemption for someone who died in 2026?

The basic exclusion amount for 2026 is $15,000,000. A smaller estate generally owes no federal estate tax, though a return may still be filed to elect portability.

Who do I contact about an old Michigan inheritance tax matter?

Write to the Michigan Department of Treasury, Inheritance Tax Section, Austin Building, 430 W Allegan St., Lansing, MI 48922, or call (517) 636-4419. Send the letter within 90 days of discovering the asset.

Will the tax bill rise after I inherit a Michigan house?

It can. Inheriting under a will or by intestacy lifts the taxable value to state equalized value, unless the heir is a spouse or a close relative who keeps the home residential.

Does a deed from the estate to my brother or sister owe deed tax?

A deed to a sibling isn't on the family exemption list, which names children, stepchildren, grandchildren and step-grandchildren. A deed with consideration under $100 is exempt, so ask the county treasurer how a no-price transfer to a sibling will be treated.

What a lady bird deed is in Michigan

It's a deed in which the owner keeps a life estate and full power to sell, mortgage or lease the home, while naming someone who receives it at the owner's death. Michigan's Department of Health and Human Services defines it as an enhanced life estate deed, also called a transfer on death deed, that lets property pass on death without probate. The owner still owns the property and can sell, rent or change it without restriction until death.

Michigan Treasury describes nearly the same picture in its principal residence exemption guidance: an owner deeds the home to another person while reserving a life estate and full power to convey during life, including selling, gifting, mortgaging, leasing or keeping the proceeds. Treasury names that arrangement a Lady Bird Deed.

The instrument still has to be a valid Michigan deed. The statutory short form for a quitclaim makes a conveyance a good one to the grantee and the grantee's heirs and assigns when it is worded in substance as a quitclaim and is signed, sealed and acknowledged by the grantor (MCL 565.152). That form alone doesn't describe a retained life estate, so the wording of the retained powers is what a Michigan attorney will draft.

Medicaid eligibility and estate recovery

Two separate rules are in play, and both come from the state agency. On eligibility, because the grantor keeps unrestricted interest in the property, a lady bird deed isn't considered a divestment when an applicant is in a divestment penalty situation.

Estate recovery is a different question. It applies to Medicaid beneficiaries who are 55 or older and received long-term care services on or after September 30, 2007. The agency defines the estate as property passing to heirs through probate, but for someone who received an asset disregard from a long-term care partnership policy, recovery applies to all assets whether or not they pass through probate (MDHHS Estate Recovery).

Recovery is deferred while a spouse, a child under 21, or a blind or permanently disabled child is living. An undue hardship waiver is possible for a home of modest value, meaning one worth less than 50% of the average home price in its county on the date of death, and the applicant must pass a means test: household income under 200% of the federal guideline and household resources under $10,000.

Transferring assets to avoid recovery can affect eligibility, and the law presumes no undue hardship when the hardship results from such a transfer (MCL 400.112g(3)(e)(iii)). Speak with a legal advisor before you sign a deed with Medicaid in mind.

Effect on the exemption and taxable value

The deed can change who qualifies for the principal residence exemption. A person who holds a life estate counts as a partial owner and is eligible if the home is their principal residence, and any ownership interest must be in writing. In the lady bird example, the person named to receive the home has no current ownership interest because the grantor keeps full control. That person becomes an owner only at the grantor's death if the grantor hasn't used the powers.

Taxable value is a separate issue. Under MCL 211.27a, a transfer of ownership uncaps taxable value in the year after the transfer. Subsection (6) defines transfer of ownership broadly, and subsection (7) lists transfers that fall outside the definition. Whether a particular deed, or the later death of the grantor, counts is a question for the local assessor.

Selling a house that has a lady bird deed

If the deed keeps the full powers described above, the grantor is the person who sells. The owner may sell or rent without restriction until death, and the retained powers include selling, gifting, mortgaging and leasing. A buyer's title company will still want to read the recorded deed itself, because a deed written with narrower powers changes who must sign.

  • Pull the recorded deed from the county register of deeds and read the retained powers.
  • Ask the title company whether it needs the named recipient's signature or a release.
  • If the grantor has died, the deed that names the recipient is the starting point, and the recipient should ask the assessor and the title company how the transfer is handled.

Michigan's simplified affidavit for small estates, court form PC 598, can be used only when no real property is in the decedent's estate, so a house isn't handled through that form.

After the owner dies

A deceased owner is no longer eligible for the exemption because the owner can't occupy the home or intend to return. The estate's personal representative or trustee must file Form 2602, the Request to Rescind Principal Residence Exemption, with the assessor within 90 days of death. The exemption is removed as of December 31 of the year the rescission was filed.

The person who receives the home and lives there can claim a new exemption by filing Form 2368 with the assessor if they meet the ownership rules, by June 1 for the summer levy or November 1 for the winter levy (MCL 211.7cc(2)). A property transfer affidavit may also be needed, so ask the local assessor which filings apply to a transfer at death.

Questions to settle before signing

The deed is a recorded legal document, and small wording differences control who owns what. Bring these questions to a Michigan attorney.

  • Which powers does the deed reserve: selling, mortgaging, leasing and gifting?
  • Does the owner want a Medicaid planning result, and how does estate recovery apply if there is a long-term care partnership policy?
  • How will the county assessor treat the deed for uncapping and the principal residence exemption?
  • Who will file the rescission and affidavit forms after death, and within what time?

Call the assessor for the city or township where the home sits, and the register of deeds for the county, for their recording and filing requirements.

Selling for cash with a deed already in place

An owner who already recorded a lady bird deed can still sell the home during life, and a cash buyer can close without waiting on a lender's underwriting. The steps are the same as any sale where the grantor signs: confirm the retained powers, order the title search, and settle any mortgage payoff at closing.

Once the sale closes, the named recipient has nothing to receive at death from that property, because the home is no longer the grantor's. If the proceeds matter for long-term care planning, talk with a legal advisor before closing, since the money, not the house, becomes the asset to plan around.

Frequently asked questions

Does Michigan call it a lady bird deed in official materials?

Yes, in two places. The state Medicaid policy glossary lists Lady Bird Deed as another name for an enhanced life estate deed or transfer on death deed, and Treasury's exemption guidance uses the term in an ownership example.

Is a lady bird deed a Medicaid divestment in Michigan?

No. Because the grantor keeps unrestricted interest in the property, the deed isn't considered a divestment when an applicant is in a divestment penalty situation.

Does the deed avoid Medicaid estate recovery?

Not necessarily. Recovery reaches all assets, probate or not, for beneficiaries who received an asset disregard under a long-term care partnership policy, so ask a legal advisor how your facts apply.

Can the person named in the deed claim the principal residence exemption?

Not while the grantor keeps full control. That person has no current ownership interest and becomes an owner only at the grantor's death if the powers were not used.

Does recording a lady bird deed raise property taxes?

That depends on whether the conveyance is a transfer of ownership under MCL 211.27a. A transfer of ownership uncaps taxable value in the next calendar year, so ask the local assessor before you record.

How probate works when a Michigan homeowner dies

Michigan handles estates under the Estates and Protected Individuals Code, known as EPIC. At death, a person's property passes to the people named in the will, or to heirs if there's no will, but it passes subject to creditors, family allowances and administration (MCL 700.3101). For a house, that usually means a probate court has to appoint someone with authority before a deed can be signed.

Probate runs through the probate court in the county where the person lived. The paperwork can be informal, handled through the court register, or formal, with a hearing. Informal is the lighter path and fits most estates where nobody disputes the will or who should serve.

  • An informal application is sworn by an interested person and lists the decedent's details, the family members and the applicant's priority to serve.
  • A formal proceeding is required when anyone objects to who is appointed.
  • If a will exists, the original goes to the court with the application.

Who can serve and sign for the house

MCL 700.3203 sets a ranking. The person named in a probated will comes first, then a surviving spouse who is also a devisee, other devisees, the surviving spouse, and other heirs (MCL 700.3203). After 42 days a creditor's nominee can be considered, and after 63 days the state or county public administrator can step in if no interested person has applied, if no heirs are known, or if no heir is a United States resident entitled to a share.

Someone who ranks high can nominate another qualified person, or renounce in writing. Objections to an appointment can only be raised in a formal proceeding. Siblings who disagree about who should serve should expect a hearing, which adds time before any listing or sale.

An interested person makes the application for informal appointment, and a creditor with a claim that can't be enforced without administration may apply if nobody has filed within 28 days after death (MCL 700.3301).

Does the small estate affidavit work for a house?

Usually not. The sworn-statement route in MCL 700.3983 requires the statement to say the estate holds no real property, and it covers tangible personal property, debts owed to the decedent and similar items, starting 28 days after death. It can't move title to a house.

The court-order route is different. Under MCL 700.3982, a court may order property turned over to the surviving spouse, or to heirs if there's no spouse, when funeral and burial expenses are shown paid and the rest of the gross estate is $50,000 or less. Since 2024, a mortgage or other debt secured by real property in the estate is subtracted from its value, up to $250,000, when the court calculates that total.

The dollar figures are adjusted for inflation under MCL 700.1210. The Department of Treasury publishes the factor each year, so ask the probate court register or Treasury for the number that applies to the year of death. An heir who receives property by this order is responsible for the decedent's unpaid debts, up to the value received, for 63 days after the order.

Selling the property as personal representative

Once appointed, a personal representative may sell, mortgage or lease estate property for cash or on credit, including land in Michigan or elsewhere, unless the will or a court order says otherwise (MCL 700.3715). The same section lets the representative insure the property, make repairs and pay taxes and other costs of administration from the estate.

Within 28 days of appointment, the representative must notify heirs and devisees and the surviving spouse of the spouse's election rights (MCL 700.3705). Heirs who stay quiet about a sale can still be owed an inventory and an account later, so keep them informed before listing.

Special limits apply when the representative is the state or a county public administrator. The court must approve any sale of real property after a hearing, and fees tied to selling a property under tax or mortgage foreclosure are capped at 10 percent of net proceeds once those proceeds pass $30,000.

If no one opens probate before the house is sold

Michigan law does allow heirs and devisees to take an estate without administration. MCL 700.3901 says a successor can establish title by proving the decedent's ownership, the death and the successor's relationship. The catch is practical: a title company or buyer usually wants a court-issued authority, and the successor still takes subject to creditors' claims and family allowances.

Creditors have a defined window. If notice to creditors was published, claims arising before death are barred unless presented within four months of publication, and known creditors get one month after notice or the four months, whichever is later. If the notice rules weren't followed, the window is three years after death (MCL 700.3803). A mortgage lender or lienholder isn't affected by that bar, since the section leaves liens on estate property enforceable.

Informal appointmentSworn application to the court registerMCL 700.3301

Steps for heirs before listing an inherited house

Work in order, because each step unlocks the next. A title company will ask for the court's letters of authority, and a buyer will ask who may sign.

  • Find the original will and the death certificate, and ask the county probate court which forms it wants for an informal filing.
  • Decide who will serve as personal representative, using the ranking above, and get any rival claimants to agree or renounce in writing.
  • Ask the county treasurer whether property taxes are behind, and ask the mortgage servicer for a payoff.
  • Keep the utilities on and the house insured while the estate is open, since the representative may insure and maintain the property.
  • Notify heirs and the surviving spouse within 28 days of appointment, then price and list the house.

An inherited house that passes to a child, parent, sibling or grandchild of the decedent may keep its capped taxable value for residential use. The property tax rules page explains how the uncapping rule treats family transfers.

What a cash sale skips for an estate

Probate comes first no matter how the house sells. Once the representative holds letters of authority, a cash sale can move faster than a listing, because there's no buyer's loan approval, appraisal or lender deadline to wait on.

  • The buyer still needs the letters of authority and the recorded deed chain.
  • The mortgage payoff and any back property taxes are paid from the sale proceeds at closing.
  • Heirs still get their notices, inventory and account, whatever the closing date.

If the estate is short on cash while it waits, remember that the representative may pay taxes and insurance from estate funds, so the house doesn't have to be sold in a hurry to cover those costs.

Frequently asked questions

Can I sell an inherited house in Michigan without probate?

Rarely in practice. Heirs can establish title without administration under MCL 700.3901, but buyers and title companies usually require court-issued authority from a personal representative. The sworn-statement shortcut doesn't apply because it covers only estates with no real property.

What is the Michigan small estate limit for a house?

The statute sets $50,000, adjusted for inflation under MCL 700.1210, and subtracts a mortgage on real property up to $250,000 when valuing the estate. The court-order route in MCL 700.3982 can reach a house, while the sworn statement in MCL 700.3983 can't.

How soon must heirs be told after a personal representative is appointed?

Within 28 days. MCL 700.3705 requires notice to heirs and devisees, and to the surviving spouse about the right of election, no later than 28 days after the appointment unless a court rule sets another time.

How long do creditors have to make claims against a Michigan estate?

Four months after publication of the notice to creditors, or one month after notice to a known creditor if that is later. If the required notice wasn't given, claims are barred three years after death under MCL 700.3803. Liens on the property aren't cut off.

Who decides who serves as personal representative?

The statute ranks the candidates: the person named in the will, then devisees, the surviving spouse, and other heirs. A court decides any dispute in a formal proceeding, and the public administrator can be appointed after 63 days if no one applies.
