What the Property Transfer Affidavit is

It is the notice a new owner gives the local assessor after any transfer of ownership of Michigan real property. The duty comes from MCL 211.27a(10), which calls for a form prescribed by the State Tax Commission.

The form states the parties to the transfer, the date of the transfer, the actual consideration paid, and either the parcel identification number or the legal description. The assessor uses it to decide whether the property's taxable value should reset for the following year.

A seller does not file it. Still, anyone selling a Michigan house should know what the buyer must do, because a missed filing can travel back to whoever failed to file on the earlier purchase.

Who files it, and with whom?

The buyer, grantee or other transferee files it with the assessing office of the local unit of government where the parcel sits. In practice that means the city or township assessor.

The register of deeds helps the assessor from the other direction. Under the same subsection, the register notifies the local assessing officer at least once a month about recorded transactions that involve ownership, and makes recorded deeds available to the county tax or equalization department. A recorded deed therefore usually reaches the assessor anyway. Even so, the filing duty stays with the new owner, and transfers that never get recorded depend on it entirely.

  • Filer: buyer, grantee or other transferee.
  • Where: the assessor for the city or township that contains the property.
  • Deadline: within 45 days of the transfer of ownership.
  • Contents: parties, transfer date, actual consideration, parcel number or legal description.

What counts as a transfer of ownership

A transfer is conveying title to, or a present interest in, property, including beneficial use whose value is substantially equal to the fee interest. A deed is the obvious case, and a land contract counts too. For a land contract signed after December 31, 1994, the taxable value adjusts for the year after the contract is signed, and recording the deed later does not trigger a second adjustment.

The list in MCL 211.27a(6) also reaches several transfers sellers sometimes overlook:

  • A conveyance to a trust, with exceptions when the settlor or spouse is the only present beneficiary.
  • A distribution under a will or by intestate succession, unless the heir is the decedent's spouse or a qualifying relative taking a residence that stays non-commercial.
  • A lease that runs more than 35 years including renewals, or one with a bargain purchase option.
  • A transfer of a tenancy in common interest, limited to the share conveyed.
  • A conveyance of more than 50 percent of the ownership of an entity that holds the property.

Transfers that are excluded

Subsection (7) lists the exclusions. They include a transfer between spouses, a transfer through foreclosure or a deed in lieu until the lender sells the property, a transfer by court judgment or order without specified monetary consideration, and a transfer given as security.

Family transfers of residential real property are excluded when the new owner is the transferor's or the transferor's spouse's parent, sibling, child, adopted child or grandchild, and the home is not used for any commercial purpose afterward. Treasury or the assessor can ask the transferee for proof within 30 days, and a transferee who ignores the request faces a $200 fine. A rental of fewer than 15 days in a calendar year does not count as commercial use for this purpose.

Even when an exclusion applies, ask the assessor whether a short filing is still wanted, so the file shows why the taxable value stayed put.

How a transfer changes the tax bill

Each year the taxable value of a parcel is the lesser of two figures: last year's taxable value, minus losses, multiplied by 1.05 or the inflation rate (whichever is smaller) plus additions, or the current state equalized value. Assessment is at 50 percent of true cash value.

A transfer of ownership lifts that protection for one step. Under MCL 211.27a(3), the taxable value for the calendar year after the transfer equals the state equalized value. After that, the annual limit applies again until the next transfer. Buyers often call this uncapping, and it is why a new owner's first full tax bill can be much higher than the seller's.

If the buyer misses the 45-day deadline

MCL 211.27b has the assessor adjust the taxable value as if the transfer had been reported. The buyer then owes the extra taxes from the date of transfer, plus interest and penalty from the date those taxes would originally have been levied, plus a daily penalty that varies by property class.

Daily late-filing penalty under MCL 211.27b(1)
Property typePenalty after day 45Maximum
Principal residence$5 per day$200
Other real property, not commercial or industrial$5 per day$4,000
Commercial or industrial, sale price $100 million or less$20 per day$1,000
Commercial or industrial, sale price above $100 millionFlat amount$20,000

The governing body of the city or township may waive the daily penalty by resolution. It cannot waive the back taxes. A buyer who disagrees can appeal the increase to the Michigan Tax Tribunal within 35 days of receiving the notice, but that appeal covers only whether a transfer happened and arithmetic errors, not the value of the home.

Can a missed filing follow the seller?

Yes, and this matters if you sold a house you once bought without filing. The levy is a lien on the property only while the non-filing owner still holds it. Once the property passes to a later buyer who did file, the earlier amounts become the personal liability of the earlier buyer who failed to notify the assessor.

The state treasurer can act as collection agent for those personal amounts at the request of the local official and may keep up to 20 percent of what it recovers. If you bought a Michigan property and are not sure the notice was ever filed, call the assessor for the city or township before you list it and ask what the file shows.

Filing the affidavit step by step

Download the current form from the Michigan Department of Treasury or ask the city or township assessor for a copy. Fill in the parcel number from the tax bill or deed, the date title passed, and the actual price paid. Deliver it to the assessor within the 45 days, and keep proof of delivery.

Recording a deed is a separate step with its own cost. The register of deeds charges $30 to enter and record a document regardless of page count under MCL 600.2567, unless a charter county has set its own schedule. Ask the register for the current fee and the accepted delivery methods. Ask the assessor whether the office takes filings by mail, in person or online, since each city and township sets up its own counter.

If you are selling for cash, the buyer still has this filing duty after closing. A cash buyer has no lender pushing the paperwork along, so it helps to mention the 45-day clock at the closing table and hand over the parcel number.

Frequently asked questions

Who has to file the Michigan Property Transfer Affidavit?

The buyer, grantee or other transferee does. The duty sits in MCL 211.27a(10), and the seller has no filing role, although a seller who bought without filing can carry personal liability for the earlier omission.

How many days does the new owner have in Michigan?

Forty-five days from the transfer of ownership. After day 45 a daily penalty starts, and the assessor can also adjust taxable value and bill additional taxes from the transfer date.

Is there a penalty cap for a family home?

Yes. For a principal residence the penalty is $5 per day up to $200. Other non-commercial property tops out at $4,000, and the local governing body may waive the daily penalty by resolution.

Does an inherited house need the affidavit?

Often it does, because a distribution under a will or by intestacy is a transfer of ownership. It is excluded when the heir is the decedent's spouse, or a qualifying relative taking a residence that is not used commercially, and the assessor may ask for proof within 30 days.

Does filing the affidavit mean the taxes go up?

A filing reports the transfer, and a real transfer of ownership resets taxable value to state equalized value for the next calendar year. An excluded transfer, such as one between spouses, leaves taxable value on the usual annual limit.

What the Michigan Tax Tribunal does

The Michigan Tax Tribunal is the independent body that hears disputes over property valuation, exemptions and special assessments once the local review has run its course. It sits apart from the Department of Treasury, the State Tax Commission, local governments and boards of review, and it hears each case fresh. Under MCL 205.735a(2), a proceeding there is original and independent and is treated as de novo, so the Tribunal does not simply rubber-stamp the board's number.

A Michigan homeowner usually meets the Tribunal after losing at the March board of review, or after receiving a notice that a principal residence exemption was denied. For a seller, the appeal matters because the assessed number feeds the tax bill the next owner inherits. The Tribunal takes a range of disputes:

  • Valuation appeals over true cash value, assessed value or taxable value.
  • Appeals of exemptions for low-income owners and for disabled former service members.
  • Other exemption appeals, special assessment appeals and classification appeals.
  • Non-property tax appeals, which have their own forms.

What comes before a Tribunal petition

For residential property, the assessment must first be protested at the local board of review. Under MCL 205.735a(3) the board stage comes before the Tribunal acquires jurisdiction, and a claim over a principal residence exemption goes to the July or December board of review first.

MCL 211.30 governs the board. Its first session falls on the second Monday of March, and a city or township can move the start to the following Tuesday or Wednesday by ordinance or resolution. That opening session starts between 9 a.m. and 3 p.m. and lasts at least six hours. During the full week the board owes taxpayers 12 hours of hearings, including three hours held after 6 p.m.

Anyone who files a protest is owed a written answer by the first Monday in June. It reports the board's action, the resulting state equalized and tentative taxable values, and the right to go on to the Tribunal, together with the Tribunal's address and the final filing date. A local unit may also allow residents to protest by letter.

Filing deadlines by property type

The classification of the parcel sets the clock, and the Tribunal cannot stretch a filing deadline. For a homeowner, the date to remember is July 31 of whichever tax year is under dispute.

MatterLast day to file

Other matters35 days after the final decision, ruling or determination
Contested tax bill (arithmetic errors only)60 days after the treasurer mails the bill

Timeliness is judged by the postmark, by hand delivery, or by the date a designated delivery service takes the package. If the final day lands when the Tribunal's offices are shut, the following business day counts. The statute also calls for certified-mail service on the respondent, with copies to the local school board secretary and, where the county is affected, its clerk.

How a residential appeal runs in Small Claims

Every residential property tax appeal can be filed in the Small Claims Division, which uses an informal process. Hearings are usually telephone calls of about 30 minutes before an administrative law judge or Tribunal member, and most owners speak for themselves. Property other than residential can join Small Claims when the tax in dispute is $100,000 or less.

The sequence after filing is short:

  • The Tribunal assigns a docket number and the local unit files an answer.
  • There is no discovery unless the Tribunal grants leave.
  • A notice of hearing arrives at least 45 days before the hearing.
  • Evidence must reach the Tribunal and the other side at least 21 days before the hearing, with a proof of service.
  • If a judge rather than a member hears the case, either side has 20 days to file exceptions to the proposed opinion, and the other side has 14 days to answer.

Expect roughly 12 to 18 months from filing to final decision, depending on docket load. If a hearing is not set until after the next April 1, the following tax year is added to the case automatically, which means evidence for both years may be due.

Uncapping and a home sale

A sale resets taxable value for the buyer, so the old owner's capped figure does not follow the house. Under MCL 211.27a, taxable value is whichever is lower: last year's figure grown by the smaller of 5 percent or inflation, or the current state equalized valuation. Once ownership transfers, the next calendar year's taxable value jumps to the state equalized valuation.

Some transfers do not uncap the property. Examples include a move between spouses, a foreclosure up to the lender's resale, and residential property going to a parent, sibling, son, daughter or grandchild who keeps it out of commercial use. The new owner reports the transfer to the assessing office on the State Tax Commission form within 45 days, and recorders send assessors a monthly list of recorded transfers.

If you own a house with an appeal still open, ask the Tribunal or your assessor how the pending year is handled once title changes hands. A cash buyer will want to know about an open appeal before closing, since a refund or a lower value could belong to either side depending on the purchase terms.

How to file and reach the Tribunal

E-filing is the preferred route and needs an account registered to a working email address. Paper petitions go to P.O. Box 30232, Lansing, Michigan 48909, to 2407 N Grand River Ave, Lansing 48906 for other carriers, or by hand to 611 W. Ottawa St, Lansing 48933. Email and fax filings are refused.

A Small Claims petition has to include the notice behind the dispute: the board of review decision, an uncapping notice, or a principal residence exemption denial, for instance. Phone 517-335-9760 on weekdays between 8:00 a.m. and 4:30 p.m., except that nobody answers from noon until 1 p.m. The staff cannot give legal advice or an opinion on whether to appeal.

Filed papers show up publicly in the docket lookup. Black out Social Security numbers, account numbers and other personal identifiers first. Owners may speak for themselves or send an attorney or other representative.

Frequently asked questions

When must a residential assessment appeal reach the Tribunal?

By July 31 of the tax year, under MCL 205.735a(6). Commercial and industrial real property follow an earlier May 31 date.

Is the March board of review mandatory for a home?

Yes for residential valuation or exemption disputes. The board stage, or the July or December board for principal residence exemption claims, must come first. Commercial and industrial owners may go straight to the Tribunal.

May an owner appear without a lawyer?

Yes. MCL 205.735a(10) allows a person to appear alone or with an attorney or another representative, and Small Claims hearings are informal enough that most owners speak for themselves.

What happens to an appeal if the house is sold?

Ask the Tribunal docket staff at 517-335-9760. The sale uncaps taxable value for the buyer in the next calendar year under MCL 211.27a(3), and the buyer sends the transfer notice to the assessor within 45 days.

How long until a Small Claims ruling arrives?

Plan on 12 to 18 months from filing to final decision, depending on docket load. Small Claims rulings typically issue within 90 days of the hearing.

Count how many $500 units the deed price holds, rounding a partial unit up. Multiply that count by $3.75 for the state tax, then by 55 cents for the county tax in a typical county. Your total is the two added together.

MCL 207.523 makes the grantor liable. Send the payment to your parcel's county treasurer within 15 days of handing over the deed. In most closings the attorney or escrow officer subtracts it from your proceeds and remits it.

Your purchase contract can push this cost to the other side, which is why every line of the settlement statement deserves a read before closing day. A buyer who covers the tax instead of the seller may file the refund request later.

Deeds exempt from the state tax

MCL 207.526 lists many exempt instruments. These are the ones that come up most for people selling a home:

  • Any deed where the price paid is under $100.
  • A parent deeding to a son, daughter, stepchild or adopted child, or deeding to a grandchild in one of those groups.
  • A transfer between spouses that creates or ends a tenancy by the entireties.
  • A court judgment or order that directs a transfer without setting a dollar price.
  • A deed that comes out of a mortgage foreclosure or stands in for one. When the foreclosing party resells, that sale is taxed.
  • A corrective quitclaim that repairs a defect in title the grantee already holds.
  • A land contract under which the vendor holds legal title until the final payment.

The county act, MCL 207.505, runs a parallel list that leaves out the child and grandchild exemptions, so have your closing agent check the deed against both.

Getting deed tax back

Sometimes. If you or the buyer paid and the deed met an exemption on the day it was signed, you can apply to Treasury for the money back. The refund right reaches back to transfers made in the four years before the amendment that created it.

One refund route is aimed at homeowners. Paragraph (u) of MCL 207.526 applies when the seller had claimed the principal residence exemption, the parcel's state equalized value had not risen above its value on the first tax day after occupancy or purchase (whichever came later), and the price was set by arm's length negotiation. Before you sign the deed, have your closing agent test your sale against that rule.

Recording fee for your deed

Recording a single document costs $30 flat, however many pages it runs (MCL 600.2567). The same section also prices these add-ons: $1 a page for copies, $5 to certify a recorded document, and records searches at 50 cents per year searched with a $5 minimum.

Charter counties can set their own schedule by ordinance or resolution, though never above their cost of providing the service. Phone the recording office covering your parcel before mailing a deed. An electronic filing must be paid for within one business day after the office receives it.

Land contracts and foreclosure deeds

A land contract where legal title stays with the vendor until the price is fully paid owes no deed tax (MCL 207.526(o)). Property tax is different. A land contract signed after 1994 is a change of ownership under MCL 211.27a(6)(b), and taxable value resets the following year. Recording the deed at payoff does not reset it again.

Paragraph (v) of that section exempts a foreclosure deed or deed in lieu from the state tax. The lender's own resale is not covered. Behind on your mortgage? Ask the county treasurer how the deed you are weighing would be taxed before you sign.

Property taxes after the house sells

After closing, the buyer gets 45 days to send the local assessor a transfer notice, on a State Tax Commission form that lists the parties, date, actual price and parcel number. Each month at minimum, the recording office sends the assessor a list of recorded transfers.

MCL 211.27a says a change of ownership raises taxable value to full state equalized value starting the next January. Giving the house to a spouse skips the reset. Since 2014 so does a residential transfer to a parent, child, sibling or grandchild who keeps the use non-commercial. How this year's bill is divided is a contract matter, shown as the proration line on the settlement statement.

Frequently asked questions

How are deed taxes figured on a Michigan sale?

Count the $500 units in the sale price, rounding a partial unit up. Each unit carries $3.75 of state tax plus 55 cents of county tax, as long as the county has fewer than 2,000,000 residents.

Is the buyer or the seller responsible for the deed tax?

Seller, by default. The statute puts it on the grantor, and it usually comes out of the seller's proceeds. Your purchase agreement can assign it differently.

How much does Michigan charge to file a deed?

Thirty dollars per document is the statutory base, and certifying a copy costs extra. A charter county may post its own schedule.

Does gifting the house to my daughter or son create deed tax?

The state side is exempt: paragraph (j) of MCL 207.526 covers a son, daughter, stepchild or adopted child, and paragraph (k) covers grandchildren. MCL 207.505 for the county tax has no matching paragraph, so ask the treasurer about that half.

What is the payment deadline for the tax?

Within fifteen days after the deed is delivered. The money usually comes out of closing funds.
